meta.title: Who really said "I am always doing what I can't do yet in order to learn how to do it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Van Gogh really wrote it — to Anthon van Rappard, Nuenen, 18 August 1885. But he wrote it in Dutch; the famous English wording is a translator's. Not Picasso.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I am always doing what I can't do yet in order to learn how to do it'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine van Gogh: letter 528 (R57) to Anthon van Rappard, Nuenen, 18 August 1885. Written in Dutch, so the famous English line is a translation. Picasso never said it.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This one is real. Van Gogh wrote it to his friend and fellow painter Anthon van Rappard from Nuenen, on or about Tuesday 18 August 1885 — letter 528 in the Van Gogh Museum’s edition, catalogued in the older numbering as R57. He wrote it in Dutch (“Maar ik maak steeds wat ik nog niet kan om het te leeren kunnen”), so the famous English wording is a translator’s sentence carrying van Gogh’s thought — and it is emphatically not Picasso’s.

source.heading: The letter

docMeta.dd: Letter 528 (529, R57), to Anthon van Rappard
Nuenen, on or about Tuesday, 18 August 1885
Dutch — “Maar ik maak steeds wat ik nog niet kan om het te leeren kunnen.”
Van Gogh Museum / Huygens ING (2009): “But I keep on making what I can’t do yet in order to learn to be able to do it.”

source.excerpt: And in drawing as well as in painting I can sometimes keep hold of certain solid and useful things, a firmer hold than you think, amice. But I am always doing what I can’t do yet in order to learn how to do it. But writing you about this bores me.
trail: On or about 18 August 1885 — van Gogh, in Nuenen, writes to Anthon van Rappard defending his method against Rappard’s criticism: “Maar ik maak steeds wat ik nog niet kan om het te leeren kunnen.” The Van Gogh Museum and Huygens ING publish it as letter 528 (529, R57) ↗.

By 1979 — the familiar English wording is in print. Quote Investigator’s earliest match is Anatole Broyard’s New York Times review of The Complete Letters of Vincent Van Gogh in three volumes, quoting “I am always doing what I can’t do yet in order to learn how to do it” — see Quote Investigator ↗.

The same wording, in the letter — the English text of R57 published by The Vincent van Gogh Gallery reads “But I am always doing what I can’t do yet in order to learn how to do it,” confirming the popular phrasing is a real translation of this passage and not a later invention: letter R57 (PDF) ↗.
By 1995 — a Usenet post credits a variant of the line to Pablo Picasso, twenty-two years after his death, with no support; QI concludes van Gogh deserves the credit ↗.
source.excerptNote: This is the English text of R57 as published by The Vincent van Gogh Gallery — the rendering that carries the familiar wording. The Van Gogh Museum’s own 2009 translation of the same Dutch sentence reads “But I keep on making what I can’t do yet in order to learn to be able to do it.” Both are faithful; neither is a sentence van Gogh wrote in English. “Amice” is the Latin vocative for “friend” — van Gogh’s habitual greeting to Rappard.

source.rightsNote: Two separate clocks run here. Van Gogh’s Dutch sentence, written in 1885 by a painter who died in 1890, is long out of copyright. The English is not: every familiar wording of this line is a twentieth-century translation. The Van Gogh Museum / Huygens ING edition carries an explicit “Copyright © 2009 Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam, Huygens ING, The Hague” ↗, and the “in order to learn how to do it” phrasing comes from a Complete Letters translation in circulation by 1979 and still held by its publisher. Short quotation with attribution is ordinary practice; reproducing the translated letter at length is not.

author.name: Vincent van Gogh
author.heading: About the author
author.bio: Vincent van Gogh (born Groot-Zundert, 30 March 1853; died Auvers-sur-Oise, 29 July 1890) is among the most famous and influential figures in Western art. He is also one of the most documented painters who ever lived: hundreds of his letters survive, including 58 to the painter Anthon van Rappard, which is why a line like this one can be pinned to a specific week in a specific village. In 1885 he was living in Nuenen, working in sombre earth tones and finishing The Potato Eaters — the very work whose reception provoked the exchange this sentence comes from.

cite.sourceCitation: Vincent van Gogh to Anthon van Rappard, Nuenen, on or about Tuesday, 18 August 1885, letter 528 (529, R57), in <cite>Vincent van Gogh: The Letters</cite> (Amsterdam: Van Gogh Museum; The Hague: Huygens ING, 2009), vangoghletters.org. The familiar English wording (“I am always doing what I can’t do yet in order to learn how to do it”) appears in the R57 text published by The Vincent van Gogh Gallery, and is documented in print by 1979.

misattribution.heading: Where it goes wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution to van Gogh is sound — unusually so for a quote this inspirational. What goes wrong is downstream: a dead painter gets the credit, and readers assume they are reading van Gogh’s own words when they are reading a translator’s.

items.why: Quote Investigator found the saying credited to Picasso in a 1995 Usenet message, in the form “I am always doing what I can not do, in order that I may learn how to do it.” Picasso had died in 1973, and QI notes the attribution “occurred after his death and was not well supported.” See Quote Investigator ↗.

items.who: An unnamed translator, not van Gogh
items.why: Van Gogh wrote in Dutch: “Maar ik maak steeds wat ik nog niet kan om het te leeren kunnen.” The Van Gogh Museum and Huygens ING render that as “But I keep on making what I can’t do yet in order to learn to be able to do it” — recognisably the same sentence, but not the wording on the poster. See letter 528 at vangoghletters.org ↗.

items.who: “Van Gogh, on painting” — usually cited with no letter, no date, no recipient
items.why: The line circulates as a free-floating motto. It is not: it has a recipient (Anthon van Rappard), a place (Nuenen) and a date (on or about 18 August 1885), all documented in the Van Gogh Museum edition as letter 528 (529, R57) ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Vincent van Gogh wrote it, in Dutch, in a letter to Anthon van Rappard from Nuenen on or about 18 August 1885 — and Quote Investigator concludes he “deserves credit for this quotation” ↗. Quote him; just remember you are quoting a translation.

context.heading: Nuenen, August 1885
lead: In 1885 van Gogh was in the Brabant village of Nuenen, painting peasants in the dark earth tones that dominated his work before Paris and Arles. That May he had finished The Potato Eaters, his first major picture. It did not land the way he hoped: his friend Anthon van Rappard — a trained painter, and one of the few colleagues van Gogh had — criticised it sharply, and the two fell out.

This sentence comes from the repair work. Writing to van Rappard on or about 18 August 1885, van Gogh defends not a painting but a method. He concedes nothing about difficulty; he insists that difficulty is the point. The line is a working principle, jotted mid-argument to one other painter — not an aphorism composed for posterity, which is precisely why it survives with a date attached.
context.detailsSummary: What surrounds the line in the letter
detailsBody: The passage begins with van Gogh conceding the job is brutal: painting peasants is “such a hard job that the utterly weak won’t even attempt it.” He claims credit only for having attempted it and laid foundations.

Immediately after the famous sentence he cuts himself off — the subject bores him, he says — and pivots to an appeal for solidarity: painters of peasants and common people should join hands rather than quarrel.
The quarrel did mend. A note to the letter points to van Gogh telling his brother Theo that the rift with Rappard was “completely made up.”
